name: Dana Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't campaign for anything. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Dana, 27, single, and I rent a room in a shared house on Orchard Lane with three other people I mostly see in the kitchen. My mum's about ten minutes away, which is handy when the money runs short. I work at Clearspring, the drinks bottling plant, on Line 4, the juice line. Seven months now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look after the labeller, which wraps the labels round the bottles, and I pull a bottle every half hour to check the fill height and the cap torque, which is how tight the cap is. When the labels start creasing I have to stop the line and call Hassan, the line lead, because I still can't always get the glue settings right. It's loud and sticky, everything smells of orange, and twelve-hour shifts kill your feet. But it's honest, and the team on Line 4 is good, we do a pizza on the last night of the rotation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a useful gadget and that's it. I use it sometimes to write emails to my landlord so I sound less annoyed than I am. At work I'd probably say we've got bigger problems, like the air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays what it is. Clearspring's already pretty automated, the filler and capper basically run themselves, so it's not AI that decides what happens to me. It's whether they put in a new line or close an old one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd try to build up some savings, because right now I've got maybe two weeks of rent in the bank. I'd ask Hassan about the next step up, which is line operator on the filler. Maybe put away fifty a month, starting after I pay off the new tyres for my car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. A bit tired, but that's the shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it depends on whether they close an old line. Is that something people talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. Line 2 is the oldest, the glass bottle line, and everyone says it's going. If it does, those people bump down onto other lines and the newest people, like me, are the ones squeezed. So I watch Line 2 more than I watch the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two weeks of rent cover if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. If the car broke down I couldn't get to the plant, there's no bus that early. I'd go to my mum, and she'd lend it, but she's on a cleaner's wage herself, so I hate asking.

S0.say: She'd call AI a useful gadget and nothing more, mentioning she uses it to write calmer emails to her landlord. At work she'd say there are bigger problems, like the air conditioning.
S0.think: She thinks her job stays as it is, since the plant is already heavily automated and AI isn't what decides her fate. What matters is whether lines open or close.
S0.do: Carries on and starts building savings from about two weeks of rent, aiming for fifty a month once her car tyres are paid off. Asks her line lead about moving up to filler operator.
S0.feel: Calm and normal, tired from the shifts.
S0.quote: So I watch Line 2 more than I watch the news.
S0.fieldNote: Dana sees her risk in plant decisions rather than in AI, and she tracks the old glass line closely. She's practical about money and uncomfortable leaning on her mother, who earns little too. Her car is a single point of failure for getting to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense, companies are going to use what saves money, and people will have to adjust. I'm not going to march about it. I'd say the smart thing is to be one of the people who knows how the new stuff works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit worried. A lot of my job is checking things, fill heights, labels, caps, and that's exactly what cameras and software are getting good at. I've got no partner's wage to fall back on and nothing much in the bank, so if my hours get cut I feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what other people on the line do first, but once a couple of them have made it work I'd follow. I'd ask to be trained on whatever new camera system they put in, and I'd use the AI to help me understand the manuals, which I already do a bit. And I'd get my forklift licence, which costs about two hundred, because the warehouse always needs drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. Like I'd need to keep my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others first. Who on the line would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hassan, mostly, he's the one who tries new things. When they brought in the new tablets for logging checks, he worked them out first and then showed us. If he says a new system is worth learning, I'd trust that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the two hundred for the forklift licence come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up an extra shift, Clearspring always needs cover in summer. Or I'd stop eating out on days off, which I do more than I should. Two or three months and it's done.

S1.say: She'd say it makes sense that companies use what saves money and that people must adjust; she wouldn't protest. The smart move, she'd say, is being someone who knows how the new systems work.
S1.think: She's privately worried because most of her job is checking, which cameras and software are getting good at. With no partner's income and little savings, any cut in hours would hit her immediately.
S1.do: Waits until a couple of co-workers make the change work, then follows. Asks to train on the new camera system, uses AI to understand manuals and pays about two hundred for a forklift licence through extra summer shifts or eating out less.
S1.feel: Anxious but not panicking, keeping her eyes open.
S1.quote: A lot of my job is checking things, fill heights, labels, caps, and that's exactly what cameras and software are getting good at.
S1.fieldNote: Her plan is cautious and sensible: follow the line lead, add a backup licence. Living alone on a low wage makes even moderate change feel pressing. She frames her politics as pragmatism, with no one to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope somebody in charge has a plan, because I don't. I'd probably say the government needs to make companies keep some people on, at least for a while. I'm not usually one for that, but two years is too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm gone, and pretty quickly. If the robots and AI can do my checks and Hassan's job too, there's no reason to keep a junior on twelve-hour shifts. And the forklift idea's no good if the forklifts drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything down to rent, food and petrol right away. I'd ask my landlord if I could move to the smaller room downstairs, which is forty a month cheaper. If I lost the job, I'd move back in with my mum and take whatever work I could, maybe cleaning with her, though even that might not last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like being on a ladder and feeling it tip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not usually one for asking government to step in. What changes your mind here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed. If it's slow, people sort themselves out, that's how it's always been. But if everyone loses their job in the same two years, there's nobody hiring, there's nowhere to move to. Somebody has to hold it together, and it can't be me with two weeks of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back to your mum's mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would feel like failing, honestly. I moved out at nineteen and I was proud of that. But she'd have me, and I'd cook for her, so it wouldn't be all one way.

S2.say: She'd say she hopes someone in charge has a plan because she doesn't. Though not usually in favour, she'd say government should make companies keep some people on, because two years is too fast.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be gone quickly, since robots and AI could replace both her checks and her line lead. Her forklift backup wouldn't help if forklifts drive themselves.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and petrol and asks to move to a cheaper room, saving about forty a month. If the job goes, moves back with her mother and takes any work, such as cleaning alongside her.
S2.feel: Frightened, like a ladder starting to tip.
S2.quote: Somebody has to hold it together, and it can't be me with two weeks of rent.
S2.fieldNote: Speed shifts her centrist view: she accepts government action because the market can't absorb everyone at once. Her backup plans collapse in this picture and she knows it. Moving home would feel like failure, softened by the idea of cooking for her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people get moving, so get moving. At work I'd say learn what you can now. I'd probably repeat whatever Hassan was saying, because he usually knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 32, and I think I'd have a few years where people are still needed to look after the new machines. If I'm one of those people, I get some good years and some savings. If I'm not, I'm in the same mess as the fast one, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the forklift licence and push to get trained on the filler and the new camera checks. Once I saw which jobs were actually lasting, I'd go for one of those, whether it's maintenance helper or the warehouse. I'd save hard, a hundred a month if I can get the operator's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know which jobs were lasting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch who gets let go and who gets kept. When they automated the old case packer last year, the person who knew how to reset it stayed and the person who just loaded it went. So I'd want to be the one who resets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in your personal life change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd stop thinking about a mortgage. I'd been half planning to save for a deposit by 30, but there's no point buying a flat if I might not have a job to pay for it. I'd keep renting.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough if people get moving and would urge co-workers to learn what they can now. She'd likely echo her line lead's advice.
S3.think: She expects a few years where people are still needed to look after new machines. If she's one of them she gets good years and savings; if not, she's in the same trouble later.
S3.do: Gets her forklift licence in year one and pushes for training on the filler and camera checks. Moves into whichever roles prove lasting, and saves around a hundred a month once on operator pay.
S3.feel: Worried but kept steady by being busy.
S3.quote: The person who knew how to reset it stayed and the person who just loaded it went. So I'd want to be the one who resets it.
S3.fieldNote: Her rule for the future comes from something she actually saw on the floor. She still waits for evidence before choosing a path. She quietly gives up her plan to save for a home deposit by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no excuse not to plan. I'd say it at work, plainly, not to scare anyone. Everyone should have something lined up by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it might be okay. Ten years is enough time to move up to operator, maybe get into maintenance, save a bit, so I'm not the junior with nothing when it lands. The end still worries me, I just can't picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my way up at Clearspring, operator in two years if I can. I'd take a maintenance course once I'd seen people from the plant do it and get somewhere. And I'd keep building savings, aiming for three months of rent, which would be a first for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait to see others do it first. With ten years, is there a risk you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yeah. But I've seen people waste money on courses that went nowhere. My housemate did a coding bootcamp for three thousand and she's working in a call centre. I'd rather be second and sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would three months of rent saved mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleep, mostly. Not doing the sums every time the car makes a noise. I've never had that, not once since I moved out.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse not to plan and would say so plainly at work. Everyone, she'd argue, should have something lined up by then.
S4.think: She thinks she might be fine: time to become an operator, maybe get into maintenance and save. The end point still worries her, but she can't picture it.
S4.do: Works towards filler operator within two years and takes a maintenance course once co-workers have proven it pays off. Builds savings towards three months of rent for the first time.
S4.feel: Uneasy, in a way she can live with.
S4.quote: My housemate did a coding bootcamp for three thousand and she's working in a call centre. I'd rather be second and sure.
S4.fieldNote: A decade suits her approach of moving once something is proven. She defends waiting with a concrete cautionary story. The idea of three months saved means sleep to her, which says a lot about her current stress.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028. I live on my own, there's no second wage, and two years isn't enough to get a single step ahead. What would help is the companies being made to keep people on, or pay them properly to leave, so there's time to find something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about living alone. Everyone plans around couples and families. When you're single on a factory wage, one bad month and you're on your mum's sofa, and nobody really talks about people like that.

headlineQuote: When you're single on a factory wage, one bad month and you're on your mum's sofa, and nobody really talks about people like that.
portrait: Dana Ziegler is a 27-year-old labeller operator on a juice bottling line, single, renting a room and holding about two weeks of rent in savings. She's practical, uses AI now and then for awkward emails and manuals, and moves once she's seen someone she trusts make a change work. Even steady change makes her anxious because most of her job is checking, which cameras do well, and she has no second income. Fast AGI frightens her and pushes her to accept government intervention she normally wouldn't. With five or ten years she plans careful steps, from a forklift licence to maintenance, and dreams of three months' rent saved.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she lives alone with no second wage and two years isn't enough to get a step ahead.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being required to keep people on or pay them properly to leave, so there's time to find something else.
